title: The provider
hook: in Persian again: He is the one who gives daily bread (Jaap)

segments.voice: Yesterday, husnal charaag, and your line, makes a room golden. Did you point out something lovely to someone? Today, the Persian lines keep going, and they come down to the kitchen table. Day three hundred forty-five.

Pick up a slice of bread and count the hands. Someone plowed a field. Someone planted the wheat, and someone else watched the sky all summer hoping it would rain. A harvester driver, a miller, a trucker on a night highway, a baker up at four, a cashier, whoever carried the bag home. One slice, and dozens of people you'll never meet. And behind them, the rain and the sun and the soil, which nobody made. Every meal is a long chain of giving. Jaap Sahib names the start of the chain. Today: the provider.
screen: `ONE SLICE OF BREAD.` → `DOZENS OF HANDS.` → `A LONG CHAIN OF GIVING.`

segments.voice: In its Persian lines, Jaap says the One is rozi dihind, the giver of daily bread, and raazak, the provider. Rozi comes from roz, a day. It means the day's portion: the food, the wages, the livelihood that keeps a household going until tomorrow. Punjabi still uses it. When people talk about earning a living, they often say rozi roti, the daily bread and the daily flatbread. Raazak is an Arabic word for the One who provides for every creature. So in the middle of all the cosmic praise, timeless, formless, sun of suns, Jaap stops at something as plain as lunch. That's very Sikh. Guru Nanak, in Japji, says there is one Giver for all living beings, and asks never to forget that One. But notice the Sikh balance. Trusting the Provider has never meant sitting and waiting. The three pillars Sikhs are taught are naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing what you have. You earn your bread honestly, you thank the Giver for it, and you share it. That's why every gurdwara has a langar, a free kitchen, where anyone can eat. The bread the Provider gives passes through Sikh hands and goes straight back out again, to whoever walks in the door. The chain of giving doesn't end at your plate. In Sikh practice, it runs through it. Rozi, the daily portion, comes in, and some of it goes on to someone else.
screen: `ROZI: THE DAY'S PORTION.` · `RAAZAK: THE ONE WHO PROVIDES.` · `ONE GIVER FOR ALL BEINGS.` · `EARN, THANK, SHARE: THE LANGAR.` · then, large: `DAILY BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the hands behind your food. Think of the last thing you ate, or hold something you're about to eat. Trace it back, one pair of hands at a time: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, who grew it. Thank each of them silently as you go. Then go one step further back, to the rain and the sun and the soil, and rest there with your breath. If you pray, you can thank the Giver of daily bread. The bell holds the time.
The provider. Rozi dihind, raazak: in Jaap's Persian lines, the One who gives every creature its daily bread.
Your line: daily bread. Today, before one meal, pause long enough to thank one person in the chain, and if you can, pass a little of it on. Day three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to earn honestly (kirat karni), remember the Name (naam japna) and share (vand chhakna), and every gurdwara runs a langar, a free kitchen open to everyone.

myth: trusting the Provider means Sikhs wait for food to arrive
Sikhs are taught to earn honestly, thank the Giver and share.
rozi comes from roz, a day
it's the day's portion: food, wages, livelihood.

and asks never to forget that One.

fork.setup: the Provider has given your household its daily bread. in Sikh practice, what happens next?
options: keep it all; it was given to you.
share it: some goes on to others, as in the langar.
refuse it until you've earned more.
fork.reveal: earn, thank, share: the bread passes through Sikh hands and back out again, which is why every gurdwara has a free kitchen.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rozi, daily bread or livelihood, a Persian word; in Punjabi, rozi roti.

trapdoor: what you thought: the provider means God hands out food.
what it means: the One is the start of the chain of giving, and Sikhs pass the daily bread on through honest work and sharing.
what a scholar hears: rozi (Persian roz, day) and raazak (Arabic root r-z-q, to provide) place a Persianate epithet beside the Sikh triad of naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna.

notes: The Jaap lines are commonly given as 'ki rozi dihind hain, ki raazak rahind hain': confirm transliteration.
Japji's 'sabhna jia ka ik daata so mai visar na jaai' is in pauri 5 (and repeated in 6): confirm.
Rozi roti as everyday Punjabi for livelihood: confirm.
Arabic root r-z-q for raazak: confirm.
